weaknesses: The main token weighting objective is technically under-specified. Eq. 6 defines phi=p(1-p) as a function of the current policy but does not apply stop-gradient, unlike the IS objective. Novelty is moderate. Dynamic SFT/RL interpolation and probability- or uncertainty-weighted supervised losses are closely related to prior work such as SRFT, LUFFY, ReIFT, UFT/BREAD, DFT, and importance-weighted SFT; the paper positions these methods but evaluates only a subset.

Experimental evidence is promising but not fully convincing. Results are reported for only two policy models and one expert source, with no seeds, confidence intervals, or statistical tests despite high-variance benchmarks such as AIME/AMC.

Baseline and model-selection protocol is unclear. The text says SFT-best is selected by peak test-set performance, while the appendix says best checkpoints are selected by validation set. This inconsistency raises concerns about benchmark leakage or inflated baselines/results.

The ablation of phi is incomplete. There is no systematic comparison against alternative detached weighting functions, clipped IS, entropy-based weights, constant rescaling of the SFT loss, or schedules that match the effective SFT gradient magnitude.

Reproducibility is limited: the implementation link is blank, dataset sampling details and validation splits are not fully specified, tool-use prompts are only referenced indirectly, and hyperparameter schedules are only partially described.

The central 'shift-readapt-overfit' motivation is plausible but mostly supported by a small number of curves rather than a systematic analysis across model families, expert distances, data sizes, and tasks.
